policies.summary: A Council site certificate binds all counties and cities as to site approval, and they must then issue the permits it addresses without further hearings; the Council may also find land use compliance despite unmet local criteria by taking a goal exception.

State land use rules cap solar PV on farmland that counties approve without a goal exception at 12 acres of high-value farmland, 20 acres of arable land and 320 acres of nonarable land, with a larger alternative path in eastern Oregon.

The Energy Facility Siting Council certificates wind plants of 100 MW average capacity or more (300 MW peak under the 3.00 wind factor), solar thermal plants of 25 MW or more, and solar PV using more than 240, 2,560 or 3,840 acres depending on land class; counties handle smaller projects unless the developer or county elects state review.

restrictions.description: City sought time to study data center and battery storage impacts and develop code amendments; contemporaneous coverage described Hillsboro as the first Oregon city to adopt a data center land-use moratorium. Active as of the July 31, 2026 research date. Effective immediately upon adoption, the resolution bars submission, acceptance, processing, or approval of new land-use applications for new or expanded data centers or battery energy storage systems as primary uses. Applications already under review are not affected. Runs 120 days (to approximately 2026-11-24) absent extension or repeal, with council review required before expiration. Legal basis: Resolution No. 2932, adopted by the Hillsboro City Council at a special meeting on July 27, 2026.

Community concern over the pace and scale of new utility-scale solar development clustered along George Millican Road (south of Highway 126 near the Prineville Airport), including impacts on wildlife migration. Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Crook County (Oregon) Board of Commissioners voted 2-1 (reported in late June 2026) to begin the process toward a potential moratorium on new commercial solar farm development, directing staff to hold public meetings and prepare draft documents. County leaders indicated the ordinance could take shape by summer 2026, but no report of a final Board vote adopting a moratorium, nor any further update on the process, was found in this pass. [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.45 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: Board of County Commissioners motion (2-1 vote, reported ~2026-06-30) directing staff to hold public meetings and prepare moratorium documents; no ordinance number exists because a moratorium had not been adopted as of this pass.

projects.description: In June 2018, a group called 1,000 Friends of Oregon filed an appeal challenging Clackamas County’s approval of a 73-acre solar project on prime farmland.
The 290-mile Boardman-to-Hemingway (B2H) transmission line, first proposed in 2007, would deliver up to 1,000 MW of renewable energy across eastern Oregon and southwestern Idaho.
In 2007, Columbia Energy Partners (“CEP”) proposed Echanis Wind Farm, a 104-MW wind farm to be developed on approximately 10,500 acres of private land.
Mountain Meadow Solar, LLC applied to Clackamas County for permission to construct a 10-acre solar farm on a parcel then used for growing Christmas trees.
The proposed 199-MW Muddy Creek Energy Park solar energy generation facility would encompass 1,588 acres.
In September 2017, Capital Power proposed a 350-MW wind project on approximately 45,000 acres in the county’s exclusive farm use zone.
Plans for the 400-MW Obsidian Solar Center in the high desert of Christmas Valley were met with opposition by local residents concerned about dust and impacts to local wildlife.
The group 1,000 Friends of Oregon filed an appeal challenging Jackson County’s approval of an 80-acre solar facility on prime farmland outside of Medford.

projects.description: In 2012, the Portland Audubon Society and Oregon Natural Desert Association filed a lawsuit in federal court to challenge the federal government’s approval of a wind farm on Steens Mountain.

Pattern Energy’s 72-turbine, 194-MW Summit River Wind project was opposed by conservation group Friends of the Columbia Gorge (FOTCG) on the belief that it would harm bald and golden eagle populations and diminish the scenic beauty of the river gorge area.
In October 2018, the state’s Land Use Board of Appeals upheld Yamhill County’s denial of a permit for a 12-acre solar project on farmland, which the owners of a nearby vineyard had opposed.

In 2025, DECH bn proposed the  Deschutes Solar and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), with 1,000 MW of solar energy generation and 4,000 MWh of storage capacity to be located on approximately 14,000 acres of private land zoned for Exclusive Farm Use (EFU) about 10 miles southwest of Maupin in Wasco County.
